justice: The street allocates most visible space to multiple wide motor-vehicle lanes, while pedestrian space is pushed to the edges under the tree belt, indicating an uneven distribution of street resources across users.

safety: Clear lane markings, a divided median, and roadside guardrails reduce head-on and side-conflict risks for drivers on this boulevard.

The roadway is very wide and visually encourages higher travel speeds, which can raise crash severity for any crossing pedestrian or cyclist.
No visible signalized crossing, traffic-calming element, or dedicated protected cycle facility appears in the image, reducing safety for non-motorized users.
livability: Tall residential towers line the corridor, indicating that housing is nearby and the street serves an inhabited urban district.
A long continuous tree edge on the right provides greenery and some visual buffering from the roadway, contributing modestly to environmental quality.
However, the scene is dominated by asphalt, barriers, and high-speed traffic space, with no visible shops, seating, bus stops, or active public-edge uses that would support daily street life.
The absence of visible people and public gathering elements makes the corridor feel more like a movement artery than a socially vibrant place.
sustainability: The substantial tree canopy along the right side and planted median strip provide urban greenery that can support shade, cooling, and air-quality benefits.
The boulevard geometry is strongly car-oriented, with several general traffic lanes and no visible transit priority or protected bike infrastructure, which weakens low-carbon mobility performance.
Dense high-rise development along the corridor may support compact urban form, which is generally more land-efficient than sprawl.

aesthetics: The avenue has a strong visual axis with repeating streetlights, median planting, and aligned tower blocks, creating a coherent and orderly composition.

The street appears clean, well maintained, and free of visual clutter such as excessive signage, litter, or damaged pavement.
At the same time, the very large expanse of asphalt and the highway-like character reduce human-scale richness and visual warmth.
comfort: The right-side tree canopy likely improves thermal comfort for sidewalk users by providing shade and reducing solar exposure along that edge.
For people in the travel lanes or on unshaded parts of the corridor, the broad asphalt surface offers little direct shade and may create heat buildup during hot weather.
The road surface looks smooth and even, which supports physical comfort for drivers and potentially for cyclists if they were allowed space, but no seating or rest areas are visible for pedestrians.

walkability: A sidewalk appears to run continuously along the right side beneath the trees, so there is at least a basic walking route separated from moving traffic.

bikeability: No dedicated bike lane, painted cycling shoulder, or protected cycle track is visible anywhere in the corridor.
The wide multi-lane roadway likely supports relatively high vehicle speeds, creating an intimidating environment for on-road cycling.
